summary: Qoheleth bids the young enjoy youth and remember their Creator before age and death come, then repeats: all is breath.

context.title: Remember your Creator before the evil days
paragraphs: The reading opens with a call to the young man to rejoice in his youth, followed at once by the warning that God will bring him into judgment. [c1] Some commentators hear the call as ironic, while Gill takes it as serious advice within limits. [c2] Many judge the chapter break at 12:1 misplaced, since the thought runs straight on. [c3]

Then comes one of the book’s three continuous sections, a description of death in 12:1-8. [c4] Commentators commonly read the failing house of 12:3 as the ageing body, the keepers as arms and the grinders as teeth. [c5] Ellicott warns that such anatomy grows forced in detail, and the Cambridge Bible notes a second line of reading: death approaching like a storm. [c6][c7]

In 12:7 the dust returns to the earth, echoing Gen 2:7 and 3:19. [c8] Ellicott sees the speaker rising here above his earlier doubt in 3:21 about where the human spirit goes. [c9] The Targum and the Talmud identified Qoheleth with Solomon. [c10] The closing refrain of 12:8 repeats the book’s opening words in 1:2, framing the whole. [c11]

translationNotes.summary: Hebel is literally a vapour or breath; “vanity” is its figurative sense, and the doubled form is a superlative.
translationNotes.body: Hebel literally means a vapour or breath, and only figuratively vanity. [c12] In Ecclesiastes it names the fruitlessness of all human enterprise and endeavour. [c13] The doubled form, breath of breaths, works as a superlative, as Gill notes: vain in the highest degree. [c14] Coming straight after the poem on death, Keil and Delitzsch hear the refrain applied not only to human works but to the human being itself. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: The participle of bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, here plural in form like Elohim.
translationNotes.body: Bôrʾeykā is the participle of bara, the verb used for creating in Gen 1:1, and it is plural in form, like Elohim, a plural of majesty. [c16][c17] The Midrash plays on its letters and finds in the word your origin, your grave and your Creator. [c18] Some Christian commentators, such as Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, took the plural as pointing to the persons of the Trinity, while others keep to the plural of majesty. [c19][c17]

translationNotes.summary: A word found only here; the ancient versions and the rabbis took it as the caper-berry, an appetite stimulant.
translationNotes.body: The word occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. [c20] The Septuagint, the Vulgate and Rabbinic usage all take it as the caper, which Brown-Driver-Briggs explains as a berry stimulating desire. [c21] Barnes pictures the berry, eaten to rouse appetite, no longer taking effect. [c22] The English desire keeps the sense but loses the image, an abstract term that the Cambridge Bible finds out of harmony with the figures around it. [c23]

translationNotes.summary: Literally “the house of his eternity”: the grave or Sheol, a phrase Jews long used for the grave.
translationNotes.body: The phrase is literally the house of his eternity, ʿôlām meaning long duration. [c24][c25] The Targum takes it as the grave, and the Cambridge Bible prefers Sheol, the dwelling-place of the dead. [c26][c27] The same commentary reports, after Ginsburg, that the phrase was in common use among the Jews of his day. [c27] It adds that the thought of immortality, though not prominent here, is not excluded. [c28]

claims.text: Eccl 11:9 calls the young man to rejoice in his youth and then warns that God will bring him into judgment for all these things.
Some commentators, such as Benson and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, read the call to rejoice in Eccl 11:9 as an ironical warning, while Gill allows it as serious advice under due limits.
Commentators judge the chapter division at Eccl 12:1 unfortunate, since the new chapter would more naturally begin at 11:9.
The Jewish Encyclopedia counts Eccl 12:1-8, a description of death, among the book's three continuous sections of considerable length.
Commentators commonly read the house of Eccl 12:3 as the ageing body, with the keepers as the hands and arms and the grinders as the teeth.
Ellicott warns that when the anatomical explanation is carried into every image, the interpretation becomes forced.
The Cambridge Bible names two main lines of interpretation: the approach of death as an oncoming storm, and a diagnosis of the bodily signs of old age.
The return of the dust to the earth in Eccl 12:7 alludes to Gen 2:7 and Gen 3:19.
Ellicott holds that in Eccl 12:7 the preacher has risen above the doubt of Eccl 3:21 about whether the human spirit goes upward.
The ancients, including the Peshitta, the Targum and the Talmud, identified the author of Ecclesiastes with Solomon.
Eccl 12:8 repeats the refrain with which the book begins in Eccl 1:2.
Brown-Driver-Briggs gives the literal meaning of הֶבֶל as vapour or breath, and the figurative meaning as vanity.
Brown-Driver-Briggs says that in Ecclesiastes הֶבֶל is used of the fruitlessness of all human enterprise and endeavour.
Gill takes the phrase “vanity of vanities” as vain in the superlative degree.
Keil and Delitzsch read Eccl 12:8 as saying that not only what man has and does, but man himself as such, is vain.
The word for Creator in Eccl 12:1 is the participle of the verb בָּרָא used in Gen 1:1.
The word is plural in form, like Elohim, a plural of majesty or excellence.
The Midrash interprets the letters of the word, finding in it thy fountain (origin), thy grave and thy Creator.
Some Christian commentators, such as Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and Gill, took the plural form as implying a plurality of persons in God, Father, Son and Spirit.
The Hebrew word behind “desire” in Eccl 12:5 is found nowhere else in the Old Testament.
The Septuagint (κάππαρις), the Vulgate (capparis) and Rabbinic usage take the word as the caper-berry, which Brown-Driver-Briggs explains as stimulating desire.
Barnes explains the caper-berry as eaten to provoke appetite and failing to take effect in an exhausted man.
The Cambridge Bible judges the rendering “desire” an abstract, unfigurative term out of harmony with the context.
The phrase rendered “long home” or “eternal home” in Eccl 12:5 literally means the house of his eternity.
Brown-Driver-Briggs defines עוֹלָם as long duration, antiquity or futurity.
The Targum interprets the house of his eternity as the grave.
The Cambridge Bible takes the eternal home as the grave or, more probably, Sheol, and reports Ginsburg's statement that the phrase was in common use among Jews of his time.
The Cambridge Bible holds that in Eccl 12:5 the thought of immortality, though not prominent, is not excluded.
